concepts.name: WPI: Definition and Conceptual Scope
key_dimensions: WPI measures price changes at the producer/wholesale level — NOT retail level (common UPSC trap)
Captures prices before goods reach the consumer, making it a leading indicator of future CPI
Covers only goods — services are excluded (critical distinction from CPI)
Published by Office of the Economic Adviser (OEA), Ministry of Commerce and Industry — NOT RBI or CSO

concepts.name: WPI Base Year: 2011-12 Revision
key_dimensions: Current base year is 2011-12, revised from the earlier 2004-05 base year
Base year selection criteria: economic stability, data availability, representativeness
Revision expanded the number of commodities from 676 (2004-05 series) to 697 (2011-12 series)
UPSC trap: confusing WPI base year (2011-12) with CPI base year (2012) or IIP base year (2011-12)

concepts.name: Three Major Groups of WPI and Their Weights
key_dimensions: Primary Articles: ~22.62% weight — includes food, non-food, minerals
Fuel & Power: ~13.15% weight — includes coal, mineral oils, electricity
Manufactured Products: ~64.23% weight — largest component, dominates index
UPSC trap: assuming Primary Articles have the highest weight; Manufactured Products dominate WPI unlike CPI where food dominates

concepts.name: Primary Articles Sub-Group: Composition and Weight
key_dimensions: Divided into Food Articles (~15.26%), Non-Food Articles (~4.29%), Minerals (~1.07%)
Food Articles include cereals, pulses, vegetables, fruits, milk, eggs, meat, fish
Non-Food Articles include oilseeds, raw cotton, raw jute, fibres — inputs for manufacturing
Minerals include metallic and non-metallic minerals but NOT fuel minerals (those go to Fuel & Power group)

concepts.name: Fuel & Power Group: Composition and Strategic Importance
key_dimensions: Includes Coal, Mineral Oils (petrol, diesel, LPG, kerosene), and Electricity
Despite lower weight (~13.15%), high volatility makes it a significant driver of headline WPI
Global crude oil price shocks transmit into WPI through this group — imported inflation channel
UPSC angle: administered prices of fuel can suppress WPI artificially (fuel subsidies masking inflation)

concepts.name: Manufactured Products Group: Dominance and Sub-categories
key_dimensions: Highest weight (~64.23%) — reflects India's industrial production structure as of 2011-12
Includes food products, textiles, chemicals, machinery, basic metals, paper products
Core WPI (WPI excluding food and fuel) is largely derived from manufactured products
UPSC trap: manufactured products weight in WPI is far higher than their intuitive importance — examinees often underestimate this

concepts.name: WPI vs CPI: Structural and Conceptual Differences
key_dimensions: WPI excludes services; CPI includes services (housing, education, health) — services ~50% of economy
WPI is a producer-price index; CPI is a consumer-price index — different price discovery points
WPI has no direct representation of rural/urban consumption patterns; CPI has separate CPI-Rural and CPI-Urban
RBI uses CPI (Combined) as the headline inflation target under Flexible Inflation Targeting — NOT WPI (critical UPSC fact)

concepts.name: Headline WPI vs Core WPI (WPI excluding Food and Fuel)
key_dimensions: Headline WPI = overall WPI including all three groups
Core WPI = WPI excluding primary food articles and fuel & power — reflects demand-side/structural inflation
Core WPI is considered a better measure of underlying inflationary trends as it removes supply-shock volatility
UPSC trap: 'core inflation' definition differs between WPI and CPI frameworks — not interchangeable

concepts.name: WPI Inflation and Deflation Episodes: Policy Implications
key_dimensions: WPI turned negative (deflation) in 2015-16 due to falling global commodity prices — India's first WPI deflation in decades
WPI deflation does NOT mean consumer prices fell — CPI remained positive simultaneously (classic UPSC trap)
High WPI relative to CPI suggests margin compression at wholesale level or supply-chain issues
When WPI > CPI, it signals producers absorbing costs; when CPI > WPI, retailers/intermediaries are adding margins

concepts.name: Frequency, Release Timeline, and Revision Policy of WPI
key_dimensions: WPI is released monthly (as against quarterly for some other indices)
Provisional data released with a lag of ~2 weeks after the reference month ends
Data is revised twice: first revision after one month, final revision after completion of full data collection
UPSC angle: WPI revisions can change the inflation narrative — final WPI often differs from provisional figures

concepts.name: Commodities Coverage: Number and Selection Criteria (2011-12 Series)
key_dimensions: 697 commodities covered in the 2011-12 series (vs 676 in 2004-05 series)
New commodities added include items reflecting current consumption/production patterns (e.g., new minerals, manufactured goods)
Selection based on: production value, trade significance, availability of regular price data
UPSC trap: WPI covers only traded goods with observable wholesale prices — non-traded goods and services are excluded

concepts.name: Weighting Methodology in WPI
key_dimensions: Weights assigned based on Net Traded Value (NTV) of commodities — value of domestic production + imports - exports
NTV approach in 2011-12 series replaced the earlier value of output approach, making weights more trade-relevant
Higher NTV = higher weight — explains why manufactured products dominate
UPSC angle: weighting methodology affects how sensitive the index is to price changes in specific sectors

concepts.name: WPI and Its Role as a GDP Deflator
key_dimensions: WPI (along with CPI) is used to deflate nominal GDP to arrive at real GDP in some sub-sectors
Not the sole deflator — different deflators used for different sectors (CPI for services, WPI for goods sectors)
UPSC trap: WPI is sometimes confused as the 'official' GDP deflator — India uses a combination approach
GDP Deflator (implicit) is broader than WPI as it covers all domestically produced goods and services

concepts.name: Producer Price Index (PPI): Proposed Replacement for WPI
key_dimensions: Government and RBI have long advocated replacing WPI with PPI, which is the international standard (used in US, EU)
PPI measures prices from the seller's perspective at the first point of sale — more precise than WPI
Unlike WPI, PPI would exclude trade and transport margins embedded in wholesale prices
UPSC trap: PPI has NOT yet replaced WPI in India — WPI remains the official index; PPI is only a recommendation/proposal

concepts.name: WPI Food Inflation vs CPI Food Inflation: Divergence and Causes
key_dimensions: WPI food inflation measures price at farm-gate/mandi level; CPI food inflation measures price at retail level
Divergence occurs due to: transportation costs, intermediary margins, storage losses, APMC regulations
High WPI food inflation signals stress for farmers (input cost rise); high CPI food inflation signals consumer burden
UPSC angle: large gap between WPI and CPI food inflation highlights supply chain inefficiencies — policy implication for agricultural marketing reforms

concepts.name: International Comparison: WPI vs PPI in Global Context
key_dimensions: Most advanced economies (US, EU, Japan) use PPI, not WPI — India and a few developing nations still use WPI
IMF recommends PPI as the standard measure of producer-level inflation for cross-country comparability
WPI's inclusion of import prices and trade margins makes international comparison difficult
UPSC angle: India's persistence with WPI despite PPI recommendations reflects data infrastructure limitations

concepts.name: Transmission Mechanism: WPI to CPI (Inflation Pass-Through)
key_dimensions: WPI inflation often leads CPI inflation by 1-3 months — used as a predictor of future consumer inflation
Pass-through is incomplete: not all WPI increases transmit to CPI due to government price controls, subsidies, and market power
Manufactured goods WPI price rise eventually passes through to CPI manufactured/core inflation
UPSC trap: assuming WPI and CPI always move together — they can diverge significantly (as seen in 2012-14 and 2020-22 periods)

concepts.name: Administrative and Institutional Framework for WPI
key_dimensions: Published by: Office of the Economic Adviser (OEA), Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), Ministry of Commerce
UPSC trap: CPI is released by NSO (National Statistical Office) under MoSPI — different ministry from WPI
Working Group/Technical Advisory Committee reviews base year revision periodically
Data collected from: manufacturers, government departments, commodity exchanges — NOT consumer surveys (unlike CPI)

concepts.name: WPI and Monetary Policy: Why RBI Shifted to CPI Targeting
key_dimensions: Pre-2014, RBI informally tracked WPI as a key inflation indicator for monetary policy decisions
Urjit Patel Committee (2014) recommended shifting to CPI as the nominal anchor — adopted under Flexible Inflation Targeting (FIT) framework
Reason for shift: WPI excludes services (50% of GDP) and does not reflect consumer welfare directly
UPSC trap: RBI still monitors WPI for understanding cost-push inflation and industrial input price trends, but CPI is the OFFICIAL target (4% ± 2%)

concepts.name: Wholesale Price Index and Supply-Side (Cost-Push) Inflation Identification
key_dimensions: Rising WPI in primary articles and fuel signals supply-side/cost-push inflation (not demand-pull)
Cost-push inflation identified via WPI is harder to address with monetary policy tools (rate hikes won't increase supply)
WPI rise in manufactured products combined with CPI rise suggests demand-pull inflation — actionable via monetary tightening
UPSC angle: WPI thus helps policymakers diagnose inflation type before prescribing policy — monetary vs fiscal/supply-side response
